title: The Sub-$6,500 Chinese V-Twin Cruiser That Looks Like A Harley Nightster - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Harley-Davidson and Indian Motorcycle still lead the game when it comes to factory-custom cruiser bikes. Even the modern cruisers with liquid-cooled V-twins, lightweight underpinnings, and top-spec electronics flaunt neo-retro designs that still turn heads more than what metric cruisers do. The most affordable Harley today is the $9,999 Nightster, which is the most affordable way to experience the Harley lifestyle. But what if we said that a similar visual and riding experience can be had for even less than the $6,799 Honda Rebel 500? What makes it more interesting is that it delivers a stronger American-style V-twin impression than long-standing metric cruisers from Honda and Kawasaki: an all-new custom-styled sub-500 cc Chinese V-twin cruiser that oozes style. The $9,999 Nightster is proof that Harley-Davidson has finally let go of its old ways and embraced modern technology and dynamics. As such, the most affordable new Harley today is crucial to the future of this legacy brand. A tractable Revolution Max V-twin engine powers it. This liquid-cooled mill displaces 975 cc and produces 91 horsepower at 7,500 RPM and 72 pound-feet of torque at 5,750 RPM. Power is sent to the rear wheel via a six-speed manual gearbox and a final belt drive system. The electronic suite is impressive too, with features such as ride modes, ABS, traction control, and the Drag-torque Slip Control System. Compared to its Milwaukee-Eight V-twin counterparts, the Nightster is notably lighter and more compact courtesy of its lighter underpinnings. Coupled with a more modern suspension setup and lighter wheels, this modern Harley is also a nimble handler. Despite all the modernization, Harley has managed to keep the Nightster rooted in a neo-retro design language with high custom appeal. This is evident in its minimal bodywork, a two-to-one exhaust system, bobber-inspired chopped fenders and drag-bar design, and a solo seat. For 2026, a cool XR750-inspired color option and tank graphic dial up its visual appeal further. Harley also offers the Sportster S, which looks more brutish and custom-inspired, but it strays a bit too far from retro styling cues, becoming a borderline roadster rather than a cruiser. Also, the Sportster S is more expensive at $15,999. While many existing metric cruisers from Japanese brands try to replicate the Harley formula, they have not quite achieved the level of compactness while still retaining the original American formula of a V-twin and low-slung attitude. However, a new player in town surprises us by one-upping the Harley Nightster and its affordable metric counterparts with custom bobber styling, gorgeous paintwork, head-turning stance, and a tiny yet versatile V-twin. Benda is a fairly new Chinese motorcycle maker in America that is producing some very interesting custom-styled cruiser bikes. Its portfolio starts with the $4,999 Chinchilla 300 and goes all the way up to the wild-looking $10,899 LFC 700, the only inline-four cruiser bike today that looks like a concept bike. Here, we focus on the most subtle-looking Benda of the lot—the Chinchilla 500, which appears to have been heavily inspired by the Harley-Davidson Nightster. It blends traditional custom-inspired design cues with modern technology, all for under $6,200. Other similarities between the Benda and Harley include a dark, aggressive cruising stance. They share a stripped-back, bobber-inspired silhouette, mid-mounted foot controls, and blacked-out components. More importantly, the Chinchilla 500's liquid-cooled V-twin and frame geometry are visually similar to the Harley's Revolution Max V-twin design. Retro custom-style cues on the Benda Chinchilla 500 include fat tires, bobbed fenders, twin shocks, and a peanut-style fuel tank. These are blended with modern visual features like inverted front forks and a liquid-cooled V-twin finished in a shade of bronze, similar to the Revolution Max on the Harley Nightster. Its unique headlamp cowling design breaks conventional design molds and gets LED lighting, just like all other lighting elements on this custom-styled cruiser motorcycle. The Chinchilla 500 looks the part — but a pretty cruiser with a weak engine is just a driveway ornament. So how does its 475cc V-twin actually perform? A liquid-cooled 475.6 cc V-twin engine powers the Benda Chinchilla 500. It produces 47 horsepower at 9,000 RPM and 31 pound-feet of torque at 7,200 RPM. Power is sent to the rear wheel via a six-speed manual gearbox and a final belt drive system. It gets a slipper clutch for smoother gear changes. The chirpy engine has an 11.5:1 compression ratio and a short-stroke design. The powertrain is capable of helping the Chinchilla 500 reach a top speed of 90 mph, which is ample for highway runs. The chunky design language also helps this custom-styled cruiser pack a sizable fuel tank. The Chinchilla 500 has a 4.2-gallon fuel tank. Benda claims that this cruiser can easily do 150 miles and up to 185 miles on a full tank of gas with mixed riding conditions. Those who focus on fuel-efficient riding can squeeze out even more miles per gallon. The Benda Chinchilla 500 is underpinned by a cradle-type steel frame coupled to an aluminum alloy swingarm to offer a balance of rigidity and weight savings. It is suspended on inverted forks up front with 5.07 inches of travel. The rear gets preload-adjustable dual hydraulic shocks with just 2.55 inches of travel. Braking duties are courtesy of 320 mm twin discs coupled to four-piston calipers. The rear gets a 260 mm disc coupled to a two-piston caliper. Its chunky 150/80 front and 180/65 rear tubeless CST tires are wrapped around lightweight 16-inch wheels at both ends. The compact nature of the Chinchilla 500 makes it highly accessible to most riders. It has a wheelbase of 61.0 inches and a ground clearance of 5.9 inches. The seat height is low at 27.75 inches, which helps shorter riders feel at ease on this cruiser bike. Furthermore, its curb weight of under 500 pounds contributes to a nimbler ride, making it comfortable for city use. The pillion seat is also fairly usable for urban needs. The technology features are minimal but cover the essentials. It features a circular three-inch TFT screen as the instrument cluster. On the safety front, it gets ABS and traction control. While we have compared the Chinchilla 500 to the Harley Nightster based solely on its looks, it actually locks horns with the more affordable metric cruiser bikes like the $6,799 Honda Rebel 500 and the $6,499 Kawasaki Eliminator. Although the Japanese rivals may offer more advanced tech, they are pricier and lack the V-twin character of the Chinchilla 500. Furthermore, the Benda cruiser is a lot cooler-looking. The only downside as of now is that the Benda Chinchilla 500 is a fresh offering from a relatively new Chinese motorcycle maker that has yet to prove its reliability. Once Benda proves its longevity, there will be no stopping this custom-styled flock of cruisers from claiming the long-standing Japanese counterparts' popularity and market share. title: Norwegians line up at memorials remembering the late King Harald V. Funeral set for Sept 9 - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
content: Norway’s royal palace says the funeral of the late King Harald V will take place on Wednesday, Sept. 9 OSLO, Norway -- Tens of thousands of Norwegians lined up Sunday in front of cathedrals and churches across the country for memorial services held for the late King Harald V, who died at 89. Harald passed away Friday and his son immediately became the new King Haakon VIII. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norway’s royal palace said Sunday evening the funeral will take place on Wednesday, Sept. 9. Mourners expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. “This Sunday is different. His Majesty King Harald is dead. A family has lost their spouse, father, grandfather, father-in-law,” said Dean Pål Kristian Balstad as he opened the funeral service in Oslo Cathedral, Norway's public broadcaster NRK reported. The royal family attended a service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo. Some Norwegians decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported. Harald's son, the new king, eulogized Harald on Saturday night. He expressed his pain over the death of his beloved father and promised to lead the country with the same dedication. “I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” Haakon said in his first speech as new king that was broadcast live on public television. Trying to hold back his tears, he vowed to give everything for the country as its king. “That means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence,” Haakon said. The new king adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity status and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world. title: Man Utd v Ipswich player ratings: Bruno Fernandes stars in Red Devils win - BBC
content: Fernandes hat-trick helps Man Utd recover to beat Ipswich Bruno Fernandes scored a hat-trick and nearly added a brilliant fourth as Manchester United came from behind to beat Ipswich. Here's how I rated the players, and how you rated them. Fernandes hat-trick helps Man Utd recover to beat Ipswich Senne Lammens: Stood firm and came out on top as Enciso charged at him. Out of his area to control and lay off a pass to Shaw at one point. 8 Diogo Dalot: So close to a rare goal with a curling left-footed effort. Defensively solid. 7 Harry Maguire: Reliable presence at the heart of the home defence, then got lucky with the deflection, otherwise his 'goal' might have been ruled out. 8 Lisandro Martinez: Experience vital on a day when the home side might have buckled. Mistake for Ipswich's late goal. 6 Luke Shaw: A difficult day for the England full-back. Struggled to deal with Fatawu. 5 Kobbie Mainoo: Restored to the starting line-up and good as ever on the ball. But United's midfield struggled to cope with Ipswich running at them. 6 Youri Tielemans: Still to find form in a Man Utd shirt. Went down too easily in the penalty area. Not secure defensively. 5 Bryan Mbeumo: Held his wide position and threatened with crosses and short passes. Unlucky Rashford's cross was deflected as he hit the bar from close range. Got his goal at the end. 6 Bruno Fernandes: Hat-trick hero. Sensational performance from the captain. Thunderous equaliser, kept his nerve with the penalty after two pre-season failures and calm third. Almost scored an outrageous fourth from halfway. 10 Marcus Rashford: First league start for Man Utd since December 2024. Got on the ball often enough and ran at the visitors' defence. Almost created a goal for Mbeumo. 7 Matheus Cunha: Began through the middle again and alternated with Fernandes as the furthest player forward. Decent. 7 A new Man Utd era - but Fernandes still sets the standard Kjell Scherpen: Superb save to deny Dalot the opener and crucial touch to deny Mbeumo an easy finish. No chance with the equaliser. 8 Dara O'Shea: Robust defensive display and did well, until Fernandes took control. 6 Issa Diop: Lot of scrambling defence for the former West Ham man but coped OK for the most part and talked the Ipswich rearguard through the game. 6 Jacob Greaves: Composed on the ball and held his position, not getting drawn out when Cunha dropped deep. Probably lacked a bit of class at this level. 6 Leif Davis: Superb pass inside Dalot to release Maeda created one good chance for the visitors. Precise execution for his goal and might have had another. 8 Marcelino Nunez: Busy, in front of defence, wants to get on ball and slot in between centre-halves. Disastrous slip at just the wrong time let Man Utd in for crucial equaliser. 6 Sasa Lukic: Excellent addition to Ipswich ranks. Had the game nous to halt the home side's momentum, even at the expense of a yellow card. 7 Abdul Fatawu: Skinned Shaw close to the touchline and then had the awareness to pick out a team-mate as Ipswich took the lead. Booked for a poor tackle on Mbeumo but overall really good. 7 Julio Ensico: Held off Shaw and Mbeumo on length-of-field run but no reward as effort lacked power. A real threat. 8 Daizan Maeda: Good early raid down the left was early sign of Ipswich intentions. Shot from angle of area threatened home goal. 7 Emersonn: Tried use his size to pin Maguire and Martinez back and relished the physical tussle with the England man. 6 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Dozens gather in Rotterdam to commemorate Norwegian King Harold V - NL Times
content: Around 60 people gathered at the Norwegian Cultural Center in Rotterdam on Sunday afternoon to commemorate Norwegian King Harold V, who passed away on Friday at the age of 89. BBC reports that the king was taken to a hospital last week for a rare blood condition called hemolytic anemia, which causes the number of red blood cells to drop. The Cultural Center was filled with Norwegians but also with the Dutch connected to the country in some way. The center, also known as Zeemanskerk, was traditionally a space for Norwegian sailors passing through Rotterdam. "It was about who he was, a people person," a volunteer at the cultural center told RTL about the stories that were shared. "Harald did not comment on politics, but he did show what he considered important. Every Norwegian was equally important to him. He always cared about everyone. You heard that reflected a lot here." A condolence book that visitors can sign has been available at the Cultural Center since Friday. According to the RTL, it has collected over 60 signatures so far.

title: Chelsea v Brighton: How the players rated - BBC
content: Chelsea maintain perfect start with seven-goal thriller Cole Palmer scored what turned out to be the decisive goal in a thrilling 4-3 victory for Chelsea over Brighton at Stamford Bridge. Romeo Lavia, Pedro Neto and Joao Pedro put the Blues 3-0 up, but Brighton reduced the deficit to a single goal through Malick Yalcouye and a Joao Pedro own goal before Palmer made it four. Pascal Gross then headed in a 96th-minute consolation goal after a dangerous long throw-in was not dealt with. Here's how I rated the players, and how you rated them. Chelsea beat Brighton in seven-goal thriller to maintain perfect start Emiliano Martinez: The new signing was thrown straight in, claiming two early crosses and making saves from Malick Yalcouye and Charalampos Kostoulas - though the former did beat him with a well-struck volley. He was tested again as Brighton pushed for an equaliser in the second half. 8 Wesley Fofana: Drove forward well in possession and helped pull Brighton players out of position in the build-up. 7 Maxence Lacroix: The new signing from Crystal Palace was confident in possession but not always convincing in a defensive display that was occasionally ragged. 6 Levi Colwill: Also looked comfortable on the ball but was caught out of position at times in new manager Xabi Alonso's system. 6 Pedro Neto: Tapped in Chelsea's second goal and put a chance on a plate for Joao Pedro. However, he was most at fault for over-committing to a challenge in the build-up to Brighton's first goal. 7 Malo Gusto: Played out of position in midfield. It was a quiet performance, but he delivered some good corners. 6 Romeo Lavia: After threatening to score from a similar situation in midweek, Lavia tapped in his first Chelsea goal after four minutes. 7 Jorrel Hato: The Dutchman provided a wonderful assist on the counter-attack while playing at wing-back. 7 Cole Palmer: Scored with a wonderful curling effort in the 75th minute. He pressed well but also missed a good chance early in the second half. 8 Joao Pedro: The Brazilian produced a clever flick for Chelsea's opening goal, showcased some excellent touches and made amends for missing a good chance by scoring the Blues' third. 8 Morgan Rogers: His powerful running down the flank set up Neto for Chelsea's second goal. He should have had another assist, but Palmer blazed his effort over the bar. 7 Josh Acheampong (on 68, Fofana): Helped steady Chelsea defensively after coming on. 6 Reece James (on 68, Neto): Contributed at both ends of the pitch and provided added energy down the flank. 7 Moises Caicedo (on 68, Lavia): His afternoon was cut short after just 11 minutes as he left the pitch in tears. 6 Pep Chavarria (on 72, Colwill): An energetic cameo and looked eager to get forward. 6 Subs not used: Penders, Gittens, Estevao Willian, Welbeck. Bart Verbruggen: Struggled when coming out to claim the ball for Chelsea's opening goal, but made several good saves later in the match. 5 Olivier Boscagli: Made little impact and was part of a disjointed defensive performance. 5 Lewis Dunk: Did not stand out and was involved in a lacklustre defensive display. Also fortunate to avoid greater punishment for a poor challenge on Joao Pedro. 5 Luka Vuskovic: Tested the goalkeeper with a long-range effort in the first half but looked unconvincing defensively. 5 Ferdi Kadioglu: Struggled to cope with the combination of Cole Palmer and Pedro Neto down Chelsea's right. 5 Pascal Gross: The German delivered an excellent cross to create Yalcouye's first opportunity of the game, and had the last word with his late goal. 7 Mats Wieffer: Failed to deal with an early corner, which led to a mix-up with Verbruggen and ultimately Chelsea's opener. 5 Maxim de Cuyper: Offered little attacking threat while operating in an unfamiliar advanced role because of Brighton's injury problems. 5 Malick Yalcouye: Produced an energetic display, registering Brighton's first shot before scoring with a first-time volley that went in off the post. 7 Diego Gomez: Brighton's most dangerous attacking player but also guilty of missing several chances. 5 Charalampos Kostoulas: Played a key role in Brighton's first goal after seeing an initial effort saved, but struggled to provide a consistent threat. 6 Ibrahim Osman (on 74, Yalcouye): Made little obvious impact. 6 Subs not used: Steele, Struijk, Hadjam, Cozier-Duberry, O'Riley, Oriola. title: Chelsea v Brighton and Hove Albion | Match | Official Site - Chelsea Football Club
content: Romeo Lavia, Pedro Neto, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer were all on target as the Blues made it three wins from three games with an entertaining 4-3 victory over Brighton and Hove Albion. We were once again free-flowing in attack and opened up a three-goal advantage after just 32 minutes. Lavia netted his first Chelsea goal to break the deadlock after four minutes, and both Neto and Joao Pedro found the net with clinical finishes from inside the penalty area. Brighton reduced the deficit before interval via Malick Yalcouye, and grabbed a second just after the hour-mark when Joao Pedro deflected a cross into our net. Yet Alonso's side, as they did against Fulham, showed the right response to pressure and, with 16 minutes to play, Palmer swept home a 20-yard strike. The Seagulls did grab a late third – Pascal Gross heading home – but it proved nothing more than a late consolation. Alonso made seven changes to the side that started our Carabao Cup second-round victory over Luton Town on Thursday Emi Martinez, whose signing was confirmed earlier in the day, started in goal. Wesley Fofana, Maxence Lacroix and Levi Colwill were the back three, with Neto and Jorrel Hato at wing-back. Lavia was partnered in midfield by Malo Gusto, and the front three was Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro. Before the action got underway, there were touching tributes to two influential Chelsea figures who passed away this summer: our second all-time highest goalscorer, Bobby Tambling, and our former chairman, Ken Bates. Both will be missed. At Fulham on Monday night, the Blues made a rapid start and were ahead inside 35 seconds. Our opener didn't arrive quite as early against the Seagulls, but just four minutes were on the clock. Neto was heavily involved, as the Portugal international won and delivered a corner that Joao Pedro met at the near post. Mats Wieffer got back onto the line to block, but a mix-up with goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen saw the ball fall to Lavia, who nudged a shot over the line for his first Chelsea goal. The Blues were firmly on top. We moved the ball confidently across the pitch and carried a threat whenever we advanced into Brighton's defensive third. And ten minutes after going ahead, we fashioned our second goal of the contest. Rogers was the creator, collecting a Joao Pedro knock-down and forcing his way past Mario Vuskovic. The England international squared the ball into the penalty area, and Neto burst forward to finish beyond Verbruggen. We should have had a third midway through the half, as Neto chased down and brushed aside Ferdi Kadıoglu and played a pass to Joao Pedro. The Brazilian took a touch, which sat down two Brighton defenders, but he guided his finish from 12 yards wide. Martinez, aside from coming to collect a couple of crosses, had little work to do in the opening half-hour. He did have to produce a smart reaction stop, though, when Yalcouye prodded a cross toward goal. Joao Pedro – booed throughout by the supporters of his former club – briefly silenced the away end with a deserved 32nd-minute goal. Hato was instrumental, exchanging passes in our half with Rogers and surging upfield with the ball. Wieffer was unable to keep up with the Dutchman, who fed the ball to Joao Pedro and the Blues' No.9 made no mistake with his finish. Unfortunately, our three-goal advantage was quickly reduced as Brighton pulled a goal back through Yalcouye, who rifled a volley in off the post after Martinez had denied Diego Gomez. Before the interval, each side created one further chance: Rogers came close for the Blues with a shot from distance that flashed past the post, while Gomez headed wide. The second period remained an open affair – perhaps too much for Alonso's liking. Brighton made better use of the space and caused the Blues problems. Many of the Seagulls' chances fell to Gomez. The Paraguayan forward dragged a shot wide before missing a close-range header from a free-kick. It was a chance he should have scored. Our threat remained and Neto did excellently once again to shrug off Kadıoglu and break into the box. His near-post effort was saved and, on the rebound, Rogers whipped a cross into the six-yard box for Palmer, who could only volley over. Martinez's first big save in a Chelsea shirt came soon after, as he reacted excellently to push wide a shot from Gomez. Unfortunately, from the resulting corner, the ball was worked to Pascal Gross, whose pass deflected off Joao Pedro and ended in our net. Alonso soon turned to his bench. Josh Acheampong, Reece James and Moises Caicedo, playing his first minutes of the season, were introduced. The booked Fofana, Lavia and Neto were replaced. Our changes didn't immediately quell the Brighton tide, and Martinez had to save well from a powerful drive from Olivier Boscagli. It was an important moment as, five minutes later, the Blues struck our fourth goal of the game. The goal had shades of our first, as Joao Pedro controlled and laid off a throw-in. This time, Palmer collected the ball, advanced 20 yards, and then curled a shot expertly beyond Verbruggen. Sixteen minutes remained – and the Blues worked hard to see out the contest. We shifted into a 5-4-1 shape, which largely kept Brighton outside our box, and enabled Joao Pedro to lead several counter-attacks, which were often stopped illegally by Brighton defenders. There were five minutes of stoppage time and it appeared there would be no more goals added to the scoreline. However, in the final action of the game, a long Brighton throw was flicked on and headed home by Gross. It proved too late to alter the destination of the points, with Alonso's side taking six from our opening two top-flight fixtures. We travel across London next weekend to face Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday 6 September. Kick-off is scheduled for 4.30pm (UK time). title: When Facebook Gets It Wrong v.1.0 - Daily Kos
content:
This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to
			publication. So apparently I owe my family connection to a 20-something’s algorithm now. Cool. Cool. Cool. Cool. Gather ’round, friends, I have a delightful little parable about the tech overlords we’ve so cheerfully handed our lives to. Some months back — and I genuinely don’t know when, because naturally no one tells you — Facebook decided my account had committed some unspecified sin against the community, and poof: four decades of family photos, my grandkids, old friends I’ve known most of my eighty-three years, all of it, gone behind a wall. No explanation. No email. Just the digital equivalent of a bouncer silently pointing at the door. I’m sure there’s a perfectly good reason. I’m sure a very serious Trust & Safety algorithm, trained by a team of extremely earnest twenty-somethings in Menlo Park, looked at my occasionally cranky political commentary and concluded: yep, threat detected, this man’s a menace. Really keeping the platform safe out there, champs. So naturally, I did what any reasonable person does: I tried to appeal. And here’s my favorite part, the bit where the whole charade reveals itself as pure theater — to appeal, you have to log in. To the account. That’s disabled. Which I obviously cannot do. It’s less “appeals process” and more a Kafka short story with a Meta watermark stamped on it. I typed in my email. My phone number. Both apparently strangers to the system now, despite years of loyal, dutiful data-harvesting on their part. Funny how the recognition only fails in the one direction that’s inconvenient for me. So I did the only thing a stubborn octogenarian with nothing left to lose does: I wrote Mark Zuckerberg an actual letter. Paper. Stamp. The whole nostalgic ritual. Addressed to 1 Hacker Way, Menlo Park — which is a real street address, and yes, I did laugh typing it. I don’t flatter myself it’ll land on his desk instead of a mailroom recycling bin, but somebody in that building will know that at least one 83-year-old in rural Oregon thinks the whole system is a rigged, unaccountable mess. That has to count for something. Probably not. But it has to count for something. Anyway — if anyone here still has functioning Facebook access and wants to forward my sister a message that I still exist, that’d be swell. In the meantime, I’ll be over here, cast out of the kingdom by a machine that can target me an ad for hearing aids with laser precision but somehow can’t verify it’s actually me trying to log in. Democracy dies in darkness, sure, but apparently so does your grandma’s Thanksgiving photo album, and nobody’s written the exposé on that one yet. We continue to be paywall-free. title: George V. Selden - Kiesinger Funeral Services
content: George V. Selden, 94, of Duryea, passed away on Friday, August 28, 2026, at Hospice of the Sacred Heart, Dunmore. He was born in Pittsburgh, PA, on September 30, 1931, and was the son of the late George D. Selden and Sophia (Dorn) Selden. George was a member of Nativity of Our Lord Parish Church, Duryea. He graduated from St James High school in Pittsburgh and joined the United States Coast Guard in 1949. He served during the Korean War and was honorably discharged in 1952. George worked and retired from the Trane Company in Dunmore. He also served for many years as a police officer for the boroughs of Duryea and Avoca and worked at the Duryea Sewer Authority after retiring. George was deeply dedicated to his town of Duryea. He was recognized as the longest-living member of Excelsior Hose Company No. 2. George was a member of Duryea American Legion Post 585 and VFW Post 283, Kingston. He was a loving husband, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, brother, and friend, and he will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved him. He was preceded in death by his son, George C. Selden, and his stepson, Kenneth Budnovitch. He is survived by his beloved wife of 57 years, Margaret Langhorn Selden; his daughter, Eva Thomas and husband Jim, of Duryea; daughter in law Janet (Ritzy) Selden of Wilkes Barre; his stepdaughter, Margaret Gray, of Duryea; and his stepson, George Budnovitch, of Virginia. Also surviving are his brother, Francis Selden, of Pittsburgh; his six grandchildren; his great-grandchildren; and several nieces and nephews. In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made to Excelsior Hose Company No. 2, 798 Foote Ave., Duryea, PA 18642. Funeral services will be held on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. from Kiesinger Funeral Services Inc., 255 McAlpine St., Duryea, with a Mass of Christian Burial at 10:00 a.m. at Nativity of Our Lord Parish Church, 127 Stephenson St., Duryea. Friends may call for visitation on Tuesday evening, September 1, from 5:00 to 8:00 p.m. Interment will take place on Friday afternoon, September 4, at 1:00 p.m. at Marcy Cemetery, Foote Ave., Duryea. The AMVETS Honor Guard of Greater Pittston will provide military honors. title: Four facts ahead of FC Barcelona v Rayo - FC Barcelona
content: FC Barcelona face Rayo Vallecano at Spotify Camp Nou on Monday, kick off 9.30pm CEST. The match, corresponding to Week 3 in La Liga, will be Barça's third game in just eight days, following the fixtures against Elche and Athletic Club, both of which ended in victories for the blaugranes. To provide some context ahead of the encounter, here are four interesting facts about Barça v Rayo Vallecano. For the third consecutive season, FC Barcelona will face Rayo Vallecano in Week 3 of La Liga. Since Hansi Flick arrived at Barça, his side have always played their third league match of the season against the club from Madrid. In the first two campaigns, the fixture took place in Vallecas; this year, it will be played at Spotify Camp Nou. In the 2024/25 season, Barcelona secured a 2-1 victory in the closing stages thanks to a goal from debutant Dani Olmo. Last season, Flick's men were held to a 1-1 draw by a Rayo side that was competing in European competition. Of the last 10 meetings between Barcelona and Rayo Vallecano, the blaugranes have won only four. In fact, Rayo are the side against whom Barça have recorded the fewest victories when comparing their last 10 matches against all of their opponents in the 2026/27 La Liga season. However, under Hansi Flick, the trend appears to have shifted. FC Barcelona have collected 10 of the 12 points available from their four league encounters with the Madrid side since the German took charge. For the second consecutive matchday, FC Barcelona will face a team with a new manager. On this occasion, Beñat San José will be in charge of Rayo Vallecano. After defeating Athetic Club and new boss Edin Terzić, the blaugranes face a team also with a coach in their first season in the post with the former Eibar man taking over from the departed Iñígo Pérez. San José, who began his coaching career at Real Sociedad, faces the difficult task of matching the standards set by Pérez, the former Rayo manager who guided the Madrid side to qualification for European competition. Rayo Vallecano will once again have a Basque coach following the departure of Andoni Iraola. The current Liverpool FC manager spent three seasons in charge of the Vallecas-based club before making the move to the Premier League. Ivan Balliu, with 167 appearances, is the sixth-most capped player in the current Rayo Vallecano squad. The full-back spent seven seasons at La Masia and also made 53 appearances for Barcelona Atlètic, the club's reserve team. The 34-year-old player, who represents Albania internationally, is now beginning his sixth season with Rayo Vallecano.

title: Sutton's predictions: Leeds v Brentford - Yahoo Sports
content: Leeds and Daniel Farke proved loads of people wrong last season. But they were pretty cagey against Nottingham Forest last week in the Premier League. They weren't very creative but then they got the job done against them in the EFL Cup in midweek and because of that I can't see Leeds losing. title: Sutton's predictions: Chelsea v Brighton - Yahoo Sports Australia
content: Brighton are off to a flying start and it was a great opening result and performance by Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, winning the west London derby against Fulham. Chelsea have got some talented players and, because they've got no European football, they're going to have a good crack in the Premier League this season. What interested me against Fulham is Chelsea didn't have a lot of possession, but they were effective when they did have possession. But Brighton are just one of those teams. I don't think I predicted a single Brighton result right last season they're just impossible to call. I really like Jack Hinshelwood he's such an exciting young player and there's a good history with his family in football and connection to Brighton. But I'm going to say Chelsea carry on this run and get the three points.

title: Manchester United v Ipswich Town: Live stream, Time & How to watch - Yahoo Sports
content: Manchester United host Ipswich Town at Old Trafford on Sunday having lost their opener 2-0 at newly promoted Hull City. Our Manchester United vs Ipswich Town prediction still favors Michael Carrick's side, who finished third last season and had 71 percent of the ball and 21 shots at the MKM Stadium without scoring any of them. Ipswich are the ones arriving with momentum. Gary O'Neil won his first league game in charge 2-1 against Sunderland, with club-record signing Emersonn scoring on his Premier League debut and Jack Clarke settling it in the 90th minute against his former club. They then beat Leicester City 3-1 in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday while resting nine of that XI. These clubs have met 59 times, with United winning 30 to Ipswich's 19 and 10 drawn. United have won four of the last five, and Ipswich have not beaten them since a League Cup tie in October 1997. The two league meetings in Ipswich's last top-flight season split the difference. Ipswich drew 1-1 at Portman Road in November 2024, which was Ruben Amorim's first match in charge of United, and lost 3-2 at Old Trafford in February 2025 to goals from Matthijs de Ligt and Harry Maguire plus a Sam Morsy own goal. This is also the fixture that produced the joint-record Premier League scoreline. United beat Ipswich 9-0 here in March 1995, Andy Cole scoring five. Manchester United Team News & InjuriesCarlos Baleba will not play. United announced the 22-year-old from Brighton on Tuesday on a five-year deal, but he is carrying an ankle ligament problem from Brighton's preseason and will train individually before joining in, with reporting pointing to the middle of September at the earliest. Manuel Ugarte is out until around April with a knee injury and Matthijs de Ligt is still working back from November's back surgery, so United's midfield is thinner than a 70 million pound signing suggests. Amad Diallo is the muddled one. He picked up an ankle injury in training before the Hull game, initial scans were reported as up to six weeks, and Carrick would only say he had "picked up a niggle right at the end of the week." One outlet has since suggested a faster return. He is not expected to feature. Mason Mount could make his season debut. He failed a late fitness test before Hull with a foot problem and has since trained with the squad. Benjamin Sesko is available and came off the bench at the MKM Stadium. Three players who started on the bench at Hull are projected to start here, and that is the more interesting story than the injury list. Lisandro Martinez and Mainoo were both being managed after late World Cup returns, and Rashford's cameo at Hull was his first competitive United appearance in 618 days. It's an afternoon kickoff in the UK, which means a 11:30 a.m. kickoff on the East Coast of the U.S. The match is on Sky Sports Premier League in the UK. Those Stateside can watch on USA. For Spanish language coverage, tune into Telemundo. In Canada, it's on DAZN and Fubo. Everyone else, head on over to LiveSoccerTV to find your viewing options. title: Tonali struggles but Gonzalez impresses - player ratings for Tottenham v Newcastle - BBC
content: Sandro Tonali joined Spurs from Newcastle United in a deal worth up to £100m earleir this summer Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa fired Newcastle United to a 2-0 victory against Tottenham Hotspur. Here's how I rated the players at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and you can see how you scored them below. Antonin Kinsky: Unlike his countryman, Lukas Hornicek, the Spurs goalkeeper had nothing to do in the first half but could only watch on as Elanga's shot went in off the post after the break before Wissa's improvised effort made it 2-0. 5 Archie Gray: Can never fault his effort but is he at his very best at right-back? 5 Micky van de Ven: The captain's first start of the season. Picked up a needless early booking, but went on to make a crucial sliding challenge to deny Wissa inside the box. 6 Jan Paul van Hecke: Got back to make a block to deny Willock. Comfort in possession allowed Spurs to bypass Newcastle press. Went close with header. 6 Andy Robertson: Carried a threat going forward in the first half but could not prevent Dedic winning a header to set up Elanga's goal. 5 Rodrigo Bentancur: Work often goes unseen. Broke up play and won ball back on a number of occasions. 5 Sandro Tonali: A shaky start as he came up against his former club for the first time. Clearly still building up fitness. At fault in build up to both goals. Ironically cheered by away fans as he came off. 4 Mateus Fernandes: First Premier League start for club. Always looked to be positive and deliveries from corners caused one or two problems in first half. 5 Pedro Porro: The World Cup winner played further forward on the right wing and had a couple of openings, seeing a shot blocked by Hall and a dipping volley go just over. 5 Omar Marmoush: Debutant was quickly parachuted into starting line-up, having tormented Newcastle so many times before with Manchester City. Hit side netting on volley. Smart reverse pass created opening for Robertson. 6 Mathys Tel: Saw one stinging effort well-saved, but also frustrated the crowd by giving the ball away. 4 Kudus (on 68, Tel): Welcome return after being sidelined since January with a serious quad injury 5 Subs not used: Dubravka, Senesi, Gallagher, Bergvall, Davies How new signing Gonzalez can be Newcastle's 'Quarterback' Lukas Hornicek: Made saves to keep out Tel, Robertson and van Hecke's efforts when Newcastle were under pressure in the first half. His save from van Hecke's header left head coach Matthias Jaissle clenching his fists on the touchline. 7 Amar Dedic: Another impressive all-round performance from the summer signing little more than a week-and-a-half into his Newcastle career. Great knock-down header to set up first goal. Tino Livramento faces a real battle to win back his place. 7 Malick Thiaw: Captain again in Dan Burn's absence. A proper old-fashioned tussle with Marmoush at times, who kept him on his toes. 6 Sven Botman: Had a shaky pre-season but looking more assured. Appears to be benefitting from a run of games with the same back four. 6 Lewis Hall: Made a huge last-ditch block inside the box to prevent Porro from getting a shot away in first half. Defensively solid and no penalty fears this time. 7 Nico Gonzalez: An impressive debut. Kept composure even after booking. A stunning cross-field ball in the build up to Elanga's goal. 8 Lewis Miley: Goes about his work quietly but keeps the ball so well. 7 Anthony Elanga: Looks a reborn player full of confidence under Jaissle. Scored his second goal in two games with a smart turn and finish in off the post. His was the name repeatedly sung by the away supporters. 7. Joe Willock: Made an instant impact after coming off the bench against Liverpool, but not as effective as a starter on Saturday. Got one of biggest cheers from Newcastle fans for a meaty challenge on Tonali. 5 Harvey Barnes: Fresh from scoring two goals in the midweek win over West Brom in the Carabao Cup, but did not offer same threat this time. Fired one effort way over and failed to pick out a team-mate on one promising breakaway after his cutback went straight into traffic. 5 Yoane Wissa: Led the line in injured William Osula's absence and repeatedly dropped deep to help his side. Clever overhead kick sealed the win. 7 Sean Steur (on 71, Gonzalez): Sent in teasing deliver with corner in build up to Wissa's goal. 7 Nick Woltemade (on 71, Willock): Header set up Newcastle's second from Steur's corner. 7 Subs not used: Jaouen, Schar, Bamba, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey, Shahar After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Norway’s new king pays tribute to his late father as tens of thousands mourn - AP News
content: Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. Norway’s King Haakon at the palace in Oslo, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Heiko Junge, Pool Photo via AP) Presiding Bishop of the Church of Norway Olav Fykse Tveit lays flowers at the Palace Square to pay respects to Norway’s King Harald V, a day after he died at 89, in Oslo, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Amanda Pedersen Giske/NTB Scanpix via AP) Flowers and cards laid at the Blue Stone in Bergen for Norway’s King Harald V on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Silje Katrine Robinson /NTB Scanpix via AP) People place flowers and flags at a memorial for Norway’s King Harald V at Slottsplassen in Oslo, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Hanna Johre /NTB Scanpix via AP) Trondheim 20260829. Flowers, candles and greetings are placed at Nidaros Cathedral following the death of King Harald V on Friday in Trondheim, Norway, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Jan Langhaug/NTB Scanpix via AP) OSLO, Norway (AP) — King Haakon VIII of Norway used his first speech in his new role to eulogize his father, King Harald V, as a loving parent and dedicated monarch a day after he died at 89. “We are in mourning. At the same time, it brings us comfort and strength to know that so many are mourning with us,” the king said wearing a black suit as his speech was shown live on public television. After Harald V’s death on Friday morning, the crown prince became King Haakon VIII immediately. He thanked the people for their outpouring of compassion and remembered what a loving father and husband Harald had been. Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially so people could light candles, and write their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books. “It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, messages of condolence, and candles. Thank you so much,” 53-year-old Haakon said, sitting on a wooden desk next to his father’s portrait and two white candles. “As king, my father represented Norway and the Norwegian people with pride and joy, through visits around the country, at events here at the royal palace, and while working on Norway’s behalf around the world,” Haakon said. “I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” he added, trying to hold back his tears as he vowed to give everything for the country in the future as its new king. “And that means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence.” Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Earlier on Saturday, the new king and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra welcomed Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway to the palace where King Harald’s coffin was lying in state, the royal palace said in a statement. On Sunday morning, the Church of Norway is holding memorial services across the country, with the royal family expected to attend the service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo, the palace said. Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, Haakon stepped in as regent on several occasions. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world. title: Sony a7R V vs a7 V vs a7R VI: 2026 - Fstoppers
content:
Choosing a Sony body in the $3,000 to $5,000 range means weighing resolution, speed, and battery life against a price that keeps shifting on the used market. The a7R V, a7 V, and a7R VI look nearly identical in the hand, yet they behave very differently once you start shooting. Having bought all three with his own money, Luca Petralia walks through the physical differences, the stills performance, and the video capabilities before landing on a recommendation tied to your budget and your work. He points out small things first, like the a7R VI's dedicated button-illumination control and its reworked mode dial with an asterisk position that stores ten extra custom setups per shooting scenario. Storage separates the tiers, too. Both the a7R V and a7R VI carry dual hybrid slots that take CFexpress Type A or SD, while the a7 V drops to one hybrid slot and one SD slot. Petralia thinks a $3,000 camera should have matched the others there, though he stops short of calling it a deal breaker. Battery life is where the a7R VI pulls ahead in a way that surprised even Petralia. The a7R V and a7 V share the older NP-FZ100 battery, while the a7R VI uses Sony's newer NP-FW100. In a week of shooting nearly 1,800 frames in a single session, he still had 40 percent left, and he simply couldn't drain it in one outing. That new battery costs more, third-party versions won't appear for a while, and it makes the body slightly larger, which meant his existing cage no longer fit. The stacked-sensor architecture drives the bigger gains: the a7R V uses a conventional CMOS sensor, the a7 V a partially stacked sensor, and the a7R VI a fully stacked one. That difference makes the electronic shutter genuinely usable on the two newer bodies, unlocking 30 frames per second at full bit depth with a blackout-free viewfinder. If you shoot in dim rooms or after dark, the dual base ISO on the a7 V and a7R VI is the spec that quietly reshapes your workflow. A single base ISO sensor is cleanest at one sensitivity, but a dual base sensor gives you a second point where the signal-to-noise ratio resets. The a7 V's second base sits at ISO 8,000 and the a7R VI's at ISO 5,000, both alongside a base of 800. That means when a scene pushes you toward ISO 3,200, you're often better off jumping to the higher base and pulling exposure back with an ND filter, shutter, or aperture, because the file comes out cleaner despite the higher number on the dial. It runs against the instinct to keep ISO as low as possible, and it's a habit worth building if either of these bodies ends up in your bag. The same thinking has spread across Sony's lineup and into rival cameras from Panasonic and Nikon, so learning to read dual base ISO now pays off well beyond these three. On video, Petralia is candid that he ran his channel on the a7R V for a year and a half without trouble. The newer sensors still change the math. The a7R V caps 4K 60p with a heavy crop, while the a7 V delivers 4K 60p with no crop using angle-of-view priority, and 4K 120p in Super 35. The a7R VI adds only a very small crop at 4K 120. Oversampling differs as well, with the a7 V pulling 4K from 7K, the a7R VI from 5K, and the a7R V using line skipping. He's clear that you won't spot line skipping in normal viewing unless you pixel-peep side by side. His verdict splits along budget and intent, and it's worth hearing him lay out exactly who each camera suits, including why a used a7R V near $2,000 to $2,500 might be the sharpest value of the three and which body he's keeping versus selling. title: Tens of thousands mourn King Harald V in Oslo as Norway enters a new royal era - NBC News
content: OSLO, Norway — Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects to Norway’s King Harald V on Saturday, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo a day after the monarch died at 89. A sea of colorful flowers covered Slottsplassen, the square in front of the palace, as a steady stream of Norwegians filed past. A palace gardener removed some bouquets on the south side of the palace to keep pathways clear, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Palace workers also collected cards soaked after a nightly downpour and dried them to preserve the mourners’ messages for posterity, NRK reported. Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially on Saturday so people could light candles, write down their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books. The coffin arrived at the royal palace Friday evening from the National Hospital in Oslo where Harald died. “It’s special, intimate, and lovely. I’m placing my right hand on my chest in gratitude to him and the royal family,” Roni Ervik, 46, told NRK as he paid his respects. He said he was also paying tribute to the late king on behalf of his family, who are from western Norway. Harald V died Friday morning and his 53-year-old son, Crown Prince Haakon, became King Haakon VIII. Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, he stepped in as the country’s regent on several occasions. Later Saturday, a choir was expected to sing in the Royal Palace Square. The new king was also scheduled to hold audiences with the speaker of Norway’s parliament, the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra also expected to attend, NRK reported. Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as king either later Saturday or in the coming days. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world. title: Anne V: Beyond the Label. - theperfectmagazine.com
content: By using this website, you agree to our use of cookies. We use cookies to provide you with a great experience and to help our website run effectively. I met Anne V the way only fashion can introduce two people. We first crossed paths in Biarritz at an exhibition hosted by art dealer Lucy Chadwick before a cruise show in April. Then again with Katie Grand on Rue Cambon. We stayed in touch. By haute couture three months later, Anne and  I were meeting for coffee at 9.45am so we could be first in line when the flagship opened. Early bird special! Minutes later, we were sharing a dressing room, half naked, trying on the same pair of jeans  and the same shearling bomber jacket.  We both bought them. Fashion has always had an addiction to labels. Anne Vyalitsyna’s greatest act of defiance was refusing to accept one. Born in Russia, Anne landed her breakthrough at 15 with the Chanel Chance campaign by Jean-Paul Goude. It came down to Anne and another young Ukrainian model, Diana Kandyba, sharing a tiny Paris hotel room while competing for the same job. ‘I got it, and she didn’t,’ Anne says. ‘I had to go back and sleep beside her. She was so happy for me. I will never forget that.’ ‘What’s yours will find you,’ Anne says. ‘What’s not yours will leave you. It taught me never to be jealous. We need to make the pie bigger, not smaller.’ From then on, Anne found herself confronting fashion’s need to categorise. Editorial or commercial. Vogue or Sports Illustrated. Prada or Victoria’s Secret. ‘I never understood why I couldn’t  be a super high-fashion girl with no eyebrows and a major red lip, then go  and do Victoria’s Secret,’ she says.  ‘I give everything when I do one, and I give everything when I do the other. Why can’t I do both?’ The gatekeepers had already made up their minds. Boxes are easier to sell than women. Because fashion has always preferred archetypes to people. ‘Being versatile backfired on me a lot,’ she says. ‘I probably could have done more major shit if I had stayed exclusively in high fashion. It was really hard for high-fashion people to accept me at a size four or six. I was doing more commercial things when I was heavier.’ While others saw a changing body, Katie Grand saw the same model. At Love, at Giles, at Marc Jacobs and at the Louis Vuitton shows she styled, she continued to back Anne. ‘Katie has always loved a woman,’ Anne says. ‘She loved me at every size and shape. I always felt there was one person who sees me.’ ‘My thirties were really fucking hard,’ Anne says. ‘People see you doing well, but they don’t always want to hear about the hard years. I was scared to turn 40 – not because I was afraid of getting older, but because I was terrified that the same energy would continue into another decade. When you’re 20 and have no money, you can sleep on your friend’s couch. At 40, with your mother and child living with you, you are not going to fucking do that.’ Anne says those difficult years taught her something fashion rarely rewards: staying in the moment. ‘I was always lucky and grateful,’ she says. ‘But when I was younger, it was difficult to stay in the moment. You completed something enormous and immediately asked, what’s next?’ Now, she says, ‘I’m having an amazing period in my life, and I’m trying to be inside it. Not rushing past it. Not asking what’s next. Just saying thank you.’ After years of being ‘incredibly frugal’, Anne bought the jacket she wore in Matthieu Blazy’s first Métiers d’Art show for her daughter to inherit. ‘Now I look back and think, holy shit, if this moment in my career had happened a few years earlier, I wouldn’t have been able to handle it. I’m grateful I had that time with my daughter. I want her to understand: this is why I do what I do. This is why I fell in love with modelling and fashion.’ She wants her daughter to one day say, ‘This is the jacket my mom wore. I was there at the fitting. I met Matthieu. I saw her wear it. And now my mom owns that jacket.’ That morning in July on Rue Cambon, we bought the same jacket. Mine was for now. Anne was already imagining who would wear hers next.

title: Interstellar Travel V: Warp Drives, Wormholes, and Halo Drives - Universe Today
content:
Welcome back to our series on Interstellar Travel, where we look at the many proposals made for sending missions to the stars since the dawn of the Space Age. In our first installment, we examined how Cold War-era developments in nuclear weapons and rockets paralleled advances in space exploration, resulting in proposals for nuclear rockets. We then examined how the creation of thermonuclear weapons led to applications in fusion propulsion. Then we looked at how the discovery and creation of positrons and anti-protons fueled proposals for spacecraft driven by antimatter propulsion. In our fourth installment, we addressed the most practical options for sending missions to interstellar space, including solar sails, magnetic sails, and directed-energy propulsion (DEP). In our fifth installment, we'll examine the most exotic proposals ever made that could (in theory) enable interstellar spaceflight someday. As we explored in a previous article, a ship relying on conventional propulsion methods would take thousands of years. And while theoretical methods exist that could shorten transits to a few decades, they would be very expensive to build and require tremendous amounts of propellant. Alas, there are always those long-shot proposals, the kind that straddle the line between science fiction and fact, that still give us hope. Among them are the warp drive, wormhole travel, and using black holes to achieve velocities approaching the speed of light. This artist’s impression shows the planet Proxima b orbiting the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri, the closest star to our Solar System. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser. As noted in our inaugural installment, there is no shortage of planets beyond the Solar System (exoplanets) that are well worth exploring. To date, scientists have confirmed the existence of 6,354 exoplanets in 4,756 star systems. In fact, that number has increased since this series began on July 31st! At that time, the census was 6,333 confirmed exoplanets in 4,747 systems. Doing the math, that means that 21 more exoplanets in 9 star systems have been confirmed in less than a month. What's more, while "Earth-like" (rocky) planets are rare, with the total still at 222 confirmations, they are surprisingly abundant in our stellar neighborhood. In fact, within 50 light-years of Earth, there are 31 known terrestrial planets, 30 of which orbit low-mass, M-type red dwarf stars. The closest of these is Proxima b, a rocky planet orbiting Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf star 4.25 light-years from Earth. Discovered in 2016, the planet has an estimated surface temperature of -39 °C (-38 °F), compared to 15 °C (59 °F) for Earth. While scientists are divided on whether this planet is habitable, there are scenarios in which Proxima b could support life. Regardless, Proxima b's proximity to Earth makes it the natural choice for an interstellar mission and likely the first stop in humanity's exploration beyond the Solar System (should that ever occur). So what can the most exotic propulsion methods ever devised do to get us there? Fans of science fiction are certainly familiar with the concept of the Warp Drive. While the idea has existed for decades, it has largely been confined to the realm of science fiction and pure speculation. It was not until 1994 that an actual proposal was made for how a warp drive could work within the realm of known physics. This proposal is credited to Mexican theoretical physicist Miguel Alcubierre, who proposed what would become known as the "Alcubierre Drive" as part of his Ph.D. studies at Cardiff University, Wales. Alcubierre described the concept in a 1994 paper titled "The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity," in which he argued that it was possible to move faster than the speed of light (FTL) without violating Einstein's Theory of Relativity. More specifically, he distinguished between Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity (SR) and his General Theory of Relativity (GR). Annotated graphic of a spacecraft within a warp bubble, showing the 1) vertical dimension (expanding spacetime), 2) interior of the warp bubble, and 3) negative dimension (contracting spacetime). Credit: Kris Holland/Matt Jeffries "When we study special relativity, we learn that nothing can travel faster than the speed of light," he wrote. "This fact is still true in general relativity, though in this case one must be somewhat more precise: in general relativity, nothing can travel locally faster than the speed of light." The concept involves stretching the fabric of space-time in a wave (a "warp bubble"), which would theoretically cause the space ahead of it to contract and the space behind it to expand. An object inside this wave could then ride it to super-relativistic speeds. As he explained it: The basic idea can be more easily understood if we think for a moment in the inflationary phase of the early Universe, and consider the relative speed of separation of two comoving observers. It is easy to convince oneself that, if we define this relative speed as the rate of change of proper spatial distance over proper time, we will obtain a value that is much larger than the speed of light. This doesn’t mean that our observers will be traveling faster than light: they always move inside their local light-cones. The enormous speed of separation comes from the expansion of spacetime itself. Since the ship is being carried along as it moves (but is not moving itself), the rules of spacetime and GR would cease to apply since this method does not rely on moving faster than light in the local sense. It is only FTL in the sense that a ship inside the bubble would reach another star before a beamed transmission traveled the same distance. The theoretical basis of this drive system, where Alcubierre proposed resolutions to Einstein's field equations for GR, is known as the Alcubierre Metric. As Alcubierre argued, quantum field theory allows for regions of spacetime with negative energy densities to exist. This is known as the Casimir Effect, the attractive force between two surfaces in a vacuum. If a "ring" of negative mass could be created around a spacecraft, spacetime could theoretically contract in front of the ship and expand behind it. As he wrote: By a purely local expansion of spacetime behind the spaceship and an opposite contraction in front of it, motion faster than the speed of light as seen by observers outside the disturbed region is possible. The resulting distortion is reminiscent of the "warp drive" of science fiction. However, just as it happens with wormholes, exotic matter will be needed in order to generate a distortion of spacetime. However, the concept has its share of theoretical challenges. According to Alcubierre's original paper, the amount of negative mass (or "exotic matter") required to achieve a warp field was beyond anything humanity could achieve. There are also many uncertainties, including violations of causality, the effect on spacetime at the destination, and whether such a system would be safe for those riding the wave. In addition, all proposed warp-drive theories violate various energy conditions. In the past fifteen years, the Alcubierre Drive has received renewed attention, thanks in large part to NASA scientist Harold "Sonny" White. Dr. White's involvement began in 2011 while preparing to deliver a speech at the first 100 Year Starship symposium, a joint project hosted by NASA and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). White chose to discuss Alcubierre's field equations, during which time he made some calculations and found that the energy requirements may actually be within the realm of possibility. In 2012, White announced that he and his colleagues at the Advanced Propulsion Physics Research Laboratory (NASA Eagleworks) had begun researching the concept. In a paper titled "Warp Field Mechanics 101," White described how his team had built an interferometer for detecting spatial distortions produced by the expanding and contracting spacetime of the Alcubierre Metric. In 2013, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory published results of a warp field test conducted under vacuum conditions, which were reported as "inconclusive." By 2019, NASA effectively ended its warp drive and advanced propulsion research after White left the agency. A year later, White began working with engineers and scientists at the Limitless Space Institute (LSI), a non-profit organization dedicated to education, outreach, and advanced propulsion methods, with the ultimate purpose of creating the first warp drive! White's research builds on the work of his colleague, astrophysicist Richard Obousy, who co-founded Project Icarus with starship engineer Kevin Long in 2009. Also in 2009, Obousy and co-author Aram Saharian released a study titled "Casimir energy and the possibility of higher dimensional manipulation," which considered how next-generation particle accelerators could produce fields that alter the density of dark energy locally, changing the expansion of spacetime. Their calculations also indicated that this could be done with a negative mass about the size of Jupiter (1.898 x 1024 kg; 4.18 x 1024 lbs). While their calculations indicated that it was mathematically possible to generate a warp bubble, the energy requirement is beyond anything humanity can currently conceive. But as White explained to Universe Today in a previous interview, he and his fellow researchers showed how reconsidering the "shell-thickness parameter" of the warp bubble could further reduce the energy requirement. In short, a thicker warp shell would reduce the strain on spacetime, thus allowing a spacecraft to achieve speeds of up to 10 times the speed of light (10 c) using only two metric tons (2.2 U.S. tons) of exotic matter. Alas, while the concept has become much more feasible in recent years, it is still a theoretical proposal. At present, scientists have not confirmed the existence of negative mass, and a proof of concept is still a long way off. Here's another staple of science fiction, one which fans are sure to recognize. To break it down, wormholes are theoretical tunnels that connect two points in spacetime. The theory emerged in the early 20th century in response to Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, which established that the speed of light could not be reached or exceeded. 
The first to postulate their existence was German physicist and astronomer Karl Schwarzschild, whose solutions to Einstein's field equation (the Schwarzschild metric) provided the first theoretical basis for black holes. A consequence of the Schwarzschild metric is what he termed "eternal black holes," which were essentially connections between different points in spacetime. Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen similarly postulated the existence of wormholes, known as Einstein-Rosen Bridges, in a 1935 paper titled “The Particle Problem in the General Theory of Relativity.” According to their paper, this bridge would connect a regular black hole (from which nothing can escape) and a "white hole" (from which nothing can enter). Unfortunately, the "bridge" is located behind the black hole's event horizon, so any spacecraft entering the black hole would be crushed into the singularity. What's more, the Schwarzschild Metric showed wormholes to be unstable, as they would collapse too quickly for anything to cross from one end to the other. For a wormhole to be stable (a traversable wormhole), it requires negative mass. While negative mass is yet to be discovered, negative energy exists in many quantum scenarios (again, the Casimir Effect), In a series of papers, Prof. Juan Maldacena from the Institute for Advanced Study and Alexey Milekhin, a graduate student at Princeton University, explored the possibility of humans traversing wormholes. In the first, "Traversable wormholes in four dimensions," they proposed how charged massless fermions could give rise to a Casimir-like energy, supporting a stable wormhole. In their second paper, "Humanly traversable wormholes,," they argued that these wormholes were consistent with the Standard Model of Particle Physics. However, they found this scenario would apply only to microscopic black holes, since the entire process is in the quantum realm. To be traversable by humans, wormholes would need to be significantly larger, requiring physics that go beyond the Standard Model. To that end, they adopted the Randall-Sundrum II model (aka. 5-dimensional warped geometry theory), from which they derived intermediately-sized charged black holes. But these would generate powerful tidal forces, so a spacecraft would need a significant boost factor to bypass them and enter the wormhole. Meanwhile, research on Einstein-Rosen Bridges by Daniel Jafferis of Harvard University showed that while possible, stable wormholes would take longer to traverse than normal space. From the traveler's perspective, virtually no time would have passed but the travel time would seem much longer to an outsider. This is consistent with General Relativity and the time dilation caused by relativistic travel. Once again, though, the issue comes down to negative mass, which is required in all cases to keep wormholes stable. Since scientists have no idea how to generate negative mass, or find it as a natural by-product of cosmic processes, wormhole travel remains the stuff of theory and science fiction. To recap, traveling to even the nearest stars beyond our Solar System is always subject to the tyranny of General Relativity. To reach a significant velocity and get there in a human's lifetime, an incredible amount of energy is required. This means a tremendous amount of propellant, tiny spacecraft, massive laser arrays, exotic physics, or a combination of these. But what if it was possible to accelerate a spacecraft to relativistic speeds without the need for propellant? This is the logic of the Halo Drive, a concept proposed by Prof. David Kipping of Columbia University and the leader of its Cool Worlds lab. Prof. Kipping described this concept in a 2019 paper, where he addressed these challenges and devised a rather exotic solution. To this, Kipping suggests a modified version of what is known as the "Dyson Slingshot," an idea proposed by venerated theoretical physicist Freeman Dyson (inventor of the Dyson Sphere). In the 1963 anthology Interstellar Communications (Chapter 12: "Gravitational Machines"), Dyson described how spacecraft could slingshot around compact binary stars to gain a significant boost in velocity. As Dyson described it, a ship would be sent to a compact binary system where it would perform a gravity-assist maneuver with the two stars. The spacecraft would pick up speed from the stars' intense gravity, adding the equivalent of twice their rotational velocity to its own, before being flung out of the system. Expanding on this, Kipping proposed that the same gravity-assist maneuver could be accomplished using a rapidly rotating black hole. This idea calls to mind the Penrose Process, proposed by English mathematical physicist and Nobel-prize winner Roger Penrose. In 1971, Penrose proposed that energy could be extracted from a black hole's ergosphere, the region just outside the event horizon. In this region, infalling matter is accelerated to velocities approaching the speed of light, emitting tremendous energy in the process. By harnessing the multi-wavelength radiation emitted by the infalling matter, an intelligent species would have a virtually inexhaustible supply of energy. In the case of the Halo Drive, however, a spacecraft would insert itself into the ergosphere, allowing the black hole's rapid rotation to accelerate it to near-to-light (NTL) velocities. And just like Dyson's gravitational machines, the spacecraft would break off from the ergosphere and travel towards its destination at incredible speeds. This power of gravitational slingshots is supported by the relatively recent discovery of hyper-velocity stars. According to research from the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA), these stars are a result of galactic mergers and interaction with massive black holes, which causes them to be kicked out of their galaxies at speeds of ~30,000 to 100,000 km/s (18,600 to 62,000 mps) - one-tenth to one-third the speed of light. But of course, the Halo Drive presents numerous challenges and some notable disadvantages. In addition to requiring a spacecraft capable of withstanding intense radiation, it would also need to be strong enough structurally to handle the stresses of the intense acceleration it imparts. The process also demands tremendous precision; otherwise, the ship and crew could be pulled apart in the black hole's maw. On top of that, there's the matter of reaching the black hole, which would require significant propellant and long transit times. Ultimately, the most exotic concepts for achieving interstellar travel suffer from the same problems as many of the less exotic ones. In short, they require tremendous amounts of energy, significant advances in science, and/or the discovery of exotic physics and matter. At the same time, these concepts remain fixed in the popular imagination and continue to be the subject of research because they instill hope. With the right scientific breakthrough and commitment, an FTL or NTL concept could be realized that would deliver us to distant worlds. The kind of hope that says "someday this will be possible" is always a welcome relief whenever we're faced with the harsh realities of spaceflight and the sheer grandeur of the Universe. Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
